name: New Hampshire

notes: Food for home isn't taxed; prepared food sold by grocery and convenience stores is a taxable meal at 8.5% (as reported), which isn't counted here.

Liquor and wine are sold through the state's Liquor and Wine Outlets at prices the Liquor Commission sets, with no sales tax; beer pays 30 cents a gallon at wholesale (RSA 178:26). Left out here; drinks served in restaurants pay the meals tax, counted in the restaurant rate.

Cigarettes pay $1.78 a pack, other tobacco 65.03% of the wholesale price, e-cigarette cartridges 30 cents a milliliter and open-system liquid 8% of wholesale (premium cigars exempt); left out here. A 2026 bill to raise the cigarette tax to $2.80 (HB 1596) was killed.
Motor fuel pays the 22.2-cent-a-gallon road toll instead, left out here.
Hotel stays, short-term rentals and motor vehicle rentals pay the 8.5% Meals and Rooms Tax; not counted here, since rooms and rentals are not among these categories.
Cities and towns levy no sales, meals or rooms taxes.
Phone and TV services pay a 7% communications services tax (RSA 82-A:3); a 2025 bill to cut and repeal it (HB 417) did not pass. Not counted here.
gaps: New Hampshire has no general sales tax. Restaurant meals (drinks served included), room rentals and motor vehicle rentals pay the state's 8.5% Meals and Rooms Tax (RSA 78-A:6), counted here on restaurant meals only; cities and towns levy no sales, meals or rooms taxes.

programs: Economic Revitalization Zones, tax increment financing districts and 79-E districts are mapped from the Office of Planning and Development's layers. The zone map doesn't match the Department of Business and Economic Affairs' list of June 22, 2026 (82 towns, 239 zones): about 14 zones it approved aren't drawn (in Hillsborough, Pembroke, Chester, Colebrook, Barnstead, Charlestown, Farmington, Loudon, Jaffrey, Antrim, Lebanon, Londonderry and Swanzey), and about 14 drawn aren't on the list and may have ended or been renamed (in Merrimack, Nashua, Portsmouth, Salem, Loudon and Chesterfield). The program runs until January 1, 2028. Thirteen towns reported a TIF district in the state's 2024 land use survey that isn't on its map (Allenstown, Antrim, Barrington, Brookline, Canaan, Farmington, Franklin, Hanover, Lebanon, Lincoln, Marlow, Nashua and Raymond). New Hampshire has no state Main Street program list (the former program's site, mainstreetnh.org, is parked); the Community Development Finance Authority's tax credits have no map.

Tilton Northfield's visitor caution draws on the lodging in its census tract (12 lodging places, 3.0 per 1,000 residents), Tilton's hotels by Interstate 93 and its outlet stores, which serve shoppers and travelers as much as vacationers; its seasonal homes (9.5%) fall just short of counting on their own, so read that caution with care.
